name: Red-Black Cobweb
description: Slastyona likes to watch life of nearby grove's dwellers. This time she watches a strange red-black spider sitting at the center of a huge cobweb. The cobweb is a set of n nodes connected by threads, each of the treads is either red of black. Using these threads, the spider can move between nodes. No thread connects a node to itself, and between any two nodes there is a unique sequence of threads connecting them. Slastyona decided to study some special qualities of the cobweb. She noticed that each of the threads has a value of clamminess x . However, Slastyona is mostly interested in jelliness of the cobweb. Consider those of the shortest paths between each pair of nodes on which the numbers of red and black threads differ at most twice. For each such path compute the product of the clamminess of threads on the path.The jelliness of the cobweb is the product of all obtained values among all paths. Those paths that differ by direction only are counted only once. Of course, this number can be huge, so Slastyona asks you to compute the jelliness of the given cobweb and print the answer modulo 10 9 + 7 .
input_specification: The first line contains the number of nodes n (2 ≤ n ≤ 10 5 ) . The next n - 1 lines contain four integers each, denoting the i -th thread of the cobweb: the nodes it connects u i , v i (1 ≤ u i ≤ n , 1 ≤ v i ≤ n ) , the clamminess of the thread x i (1 ≤ x ≤ 10 9 + 6) , and the color of the thread c i ( ). The red color is denoted by 0 , and the black color is denoted by 1 .
output_specification: Print single integer the jelliness of the cobweb modulo 10 9 + 7 . If there are no paths such that the numbers of red and black threads differ at most twice, print 1 .
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 833D — Red-Black Cobweb [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
